personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Avery is sketched through a small but meaningful set of data points. He is a Death Eater who escaped post-Voldemort justice by claiming Imperius Curse coercion (GoF, Sirius's account), a known coward and opportunist who 'wormed his way out of trouble.' He appears as a cringing supplicant in GoF's graveyard scene, where Voldemort publicly humiliates him for providing false intelligence about Bode. He grovels and begs for forgiveness, receiving only the promise of prolonged punishment. In OotP he is referenced as the conduit of the Bode misidentification error, an active but failed agent. As a young man in HBP's Slughorn flashback, he is one of Riddle's social circle, present at Slughorn's gatherings — a follower who moves in elite, dangerous company. Lily Evans in a Deathly Hallows memory condemns him alongside Mulciber as someone whose 'idea of humor is just evil,' implying a pattern of cruelty and dark inclination from youth. The composite personality is: sycophantic, cowardly under pressure, cruel by inclination, and a willing Death Eater who nonetheless lacks the fanaticism that would preclude self-preservation. His voice is never heard directly in a meaningful exchange; his personality is conveyed through others' descriptions and his reaction to Voldemort's rage.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the films, Avery is a name mentioned once in passing by Slughorn in the Half-Blood Prince flashback scene: 'Lestrange, Avery, don't forget your essays.' This appears in both versions of the memory (the falsified and the true version). He is otherwise entirely absent from the film corpus. There is no graveyard scene dialogue, no punishment sequence, no reference to his cowardice, no Lily Evans condemnation, no OotP plot involvement. He is a name on a list of students.
personality_voice.difference: The film provides zero characterization. The books establish a coherent, if minor, personality profile: cowardly, opportunistic, cruel by inclination, sycophantic under authority, willing Death Eater who betrays when self-interest demands. None of this survives into the films. The one film appearance is a throwaway name-check that communicates nothing about personality or voice.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: This cannot be scored as faithful simply because the name appears. The scoring rubric requires that personality and voice be evaluable from observable evidence. The film provides no observable evidence of any personality trait. The score of 10 reflects that the character remains nominally present (the name exists, placing him in Riddle's orbit at Hogwarts) but with complete loss of every established trait. Per the rubric, 10-13 applies when 'personality is substantially altered in several important scenes'; here it is not altered but absent. A score toward the lower end of that band (10) is appropriate given that even the minimal contextual placement — Slughorn's student, future Death Eater — is preserved by implication of the setting, but nothing substantive.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced: Avery's name appears once in the film (Slughorn's dismissal). All book characterization is directly evidenced in the book corpus. The absence of film characterization is directly evidenced by the film corpus.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Avery serves several distinct narrative functions across multiple books. (1) In GoF, he is a named Death Eater at the graveyard resurrection, functioning as a concrete example of Death Eaters who avoided justice through false claims — a narrative point that establishes Voldemort's circle's moral corruption and the Ministry's failure. (2) In GoF/OotP, he is an active agent in Voldemort's intelligence network, having provided the (false) information that Bode could retrieve the prophecy — a plot-relevant error that led to Bode's incapacitation and death. He is summoned by Voldemort and presumably punished for this failure. His agency here is real: he gave orders, provided intelligence, and set events in motion. (3) In HBP, he is part of Riddle's schoolboy circle at Slughorn's gatherings — a background figure but present at the scene that defines Voldemort's recruitment of future Death Eaters. (4) In DH, he is named by Snape as one of those who 'did not attempt to find' Voldemort after his fall — a structural point about Death Eater loyalty. (5) In DH's Snape memory, Lily condemns him and Mulciber, making him part of the moral pressure on Snape's choices.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, Avery has no narrative function whatsoever beyond occupying a seat in Slughorn's office as a named student. He does not appear at the graveyard, is not referenced in OotP's plot around the prophecy, is not named by Snape or Lily, and plays no role in any plot development. The Bode intelligence subplot is entirely absent from the films.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Every plot-active role Avery holds in the books is removed. His function as a named Death Eater at the resurrection, his role in the Bode plan and its failure, his presence in Snape's memory via Lily's condemnation — all absent. His only film appearance reduces him to background noise in a scene centered on Riddle.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The rubric penalizes when agency is removed even if the character still appears in a scene, and when the character is reduced to decoration. Avery in the films is exactly that: decoration. His book narrative functions — intelligence agent, failed operative, graveyard Death Eater, moral pressure on Snape — are either removed or not transferred to him. Score of 7 reflects that his role is 'heavily substituted, weakened, or reassigned' per the 6-9 band, with the slight upward adjustment because he retains nominal presence in Riddle's pre-Death Eater circle.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced: all book roles are evidenced in the corpus. Film absence is directly evidenced.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: The books establish Avery's motivations with limited but clear strokes: self-preservation (claiming Imperius to avoid Azkaban), desire for standing within Voldemort's inner circle (active intelligence work in OotP), and the social/ideological pull of dark magic from his Hogwarts years (Lily's condemnation of his and Mulciber's 'evil' humor). There is a minimal but readable internal logic: a man drawn to power and cruelty who will nonetheless abandon ideology when facing personal cost. No deep internal conflict is shown, but the pattern of behavior implies a character motivated primarily by self-interest dressed in Death Eater loyalty.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: No motivations are conveyed in the films. The single name-check provides no basis for inferring motivation.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: All motivational context — self-preservation, opportunistic loyalty, attraction to dark magic — is absent from the films.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are not simplified; they are entirely absent. This falls into the 5-7 band ('motivations are mostly wrong or replaced') at the lower end, since there is no replacement — simply absence. Score of 7.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Book motivations: directly evidenced and reasonably inferred from corpus. Film motivations: not enough evidence.

character_arc.book_baseline: Avery's arc, such as it is, runs from ambitious Hogwarts student in Riddle's inner circle (HBP flashback, DH Snape memory) to active Death Eater, to opportunistic defector claiming Imperius after Voldemort's fall, to reinstated but punished operative in GoF/OotP. It is a minor arc of moral degradation followed by cowardly self-preservation, concluding with re-subjugation under a returned Voldemort. This is a flat arc in terms of internal growth — Avery does not change meaningfully — but it has structural progression across time.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films show only one point of this arc: a teenage Avery in Riddle's school circle. No subsequent development is shown.
character_arc.difference: The arc's later stages — Death Eater service, defection, Imperius claim, punishment under Voldemort — are entirely absent. Only the starting point (tangentially) exists.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete to the point of being non-functional in the films. Only the earliest stage is present, and even that is not framed as part of Avery's arc but as background to Riddle's. Score of 6 reflects 'arc is significantly altered' — in practice, it does not exist as an arc in the films.
character_arc.evidence_status: Book arc: directly evidenced across corpus. Film arc: not enough evidence to establish any arc.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Avery's key relationships in the books are: (1) Voldemort — a relationship of fearful subordination, with Avery groveling and being punished; the power dynamic is absolute and one-directional. (2) The broader Death Eater circle — Avery is named alongside Nott, Crabbe, Goyle, Rosier, Wilkes, Lestranges, establishing him as a peer within that group. (3) Young Tom Riddle's Hogwarts circle — present in Slughorn's gatherings. (4) Snape, indirectly — Lily condemns Avery and Mulciber in the same breath as criticizing Snape's friendships, making Avery part of the social pressure on Snape. (5) Mulciber — explicitly paired with him by Lily as sharing a taste for evil.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The only relationship implied by the films is Avery's membership in Riddle's school circle, conveyed solely by his name being mentioned alongside Lestrange in Slughorn's dismissal. No dynamic, no interaction, no emotional register is shown.
key_relationships.difference: The Voldemort subordination dynamic — the most dramatically charged relationship — is entirely absent. The Snape/Lily social pressure dynamic is absent. The pairing with Mulciber is absent. Only a vestigial, uncharacterized membership in Riddle's circle remains.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationship dynamics are not preserved; they are absent. The score of 5 reflects 'important relationship dynamics are altered or weakened' — in practice absent, but the nominal placement in Riddle's circle prevents a score of 3-4 which implies active mischaracterization.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Book relationships: directly evidenced. Film relationships: not enough evidence beyond nominal placement.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Avery's book complexity is limited but real: the coward who claims Imperius while others go to Azkaban, the active intelligence operative who fails and is punished, the young man in Riddle's circle condemned by Lily as 'evil,' the Death Eater named by Snape as one who did not search for Voldemort. These elements together create a coherent, if minor, portrait of moral compromise, self-interest, cruelty, and cowardice. He is not a flat villain — he is specifically the kind of Death Eater who survives through calculation rather than fanaticism.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: No complexity or nuance survives. The character is a name in a list.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: All defining material — the Imperius cowardice, the punishment scene, the Bode intelligence failure, the Lily condemnation — is absent. None of it is replaced or compensated for.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The rubric states: penalize when absence changes, simplifies, or weakens the character's book characterization. Here the absence is total. The character is reduced to a name, which is the most extreme form of simplification. Score of 5 reflects 'major flattening; character is reduced to a simpler function or trait' — in this case, reduced below even a function, to a mere signifier of group membership.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Book complexity: directly evidenced. Film complexity: not enough evidence.

comparative.key_observations: Avery is a minor but textually coherent character in the books, defined across four books by a consistent pattern: a cowardly, self-preserving, cruel-by-inclination Death Eater who escapes justice through calculated deception, fails Voldemort as an intelligence operative, and is part of the social fabric that shaped Snape's moral trajectory. The films reduce him to a single name-drop in Slughorn's office during the HBP flashback, conveying nothing about his personality, motivations, relationships, or narrative function. The score of 40 reflects that his nominal presence is preserved (he exists as a name in Riddle's circle) but essentially nothing that defines him as a character in the books survives. Confidence is uniformly Low because the film corpus provides almost no material to evaluate — the score is based primarily on the near-total absence of film characterization rather than on detailed comparative analysis. A character with this little film material cannot score higher without faithful representation of at least some defining traits; none are present.
